chapter: Blues, American music and musicians' backgrounds
title: Do humble backgrounds shape musicians? The keyhole to studio work
summary: Great musicians mostly came from humble backgrounds; studio players converged on music centers and competed through a keyhole.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Good answer. I’m not sure I can verbalize this question, but sometimes I read sociologists writing about music and then you read musicians talking about where their music came from. And a lot of times they’re not sort of on the same page. I wonder how much you feel the social conditions that musicians grow up in affects their musicianship.

Good question. Well if you look at the greats, the legends, they certainly didn’t come from affluent background. Louis Armstrong certainly didn’t. Hank Williams certainly didn’t. I think you go to any great legendary musician and it usually comes — I mean Dolly, very humble backgrounds. You’re talking about I mean really humble backgrounds, and a lot of these people, whether it’s country, blues, jazz, rock & roll, Elvis certainly didn’t come from an affluent background. He was influenced by Chuck Berry and Fats Domino and Little Richard. They certainly didn’t come from affluent backgrounds nor did James Brown. So I think it has a huge impact on the musician coming up from humble backgrounds. But then again, look at the person who really had such an impact on society, John Hammond, did come from an affluent background but he was not a musician. But he recognized good musicians and had great ears, but came from a very affluent background. That’s why he was able to pay for those early records. But the musicians — I can’t say there’s no musician I’ve ever met who didn’t come from a wealthy family, maybe, but we never talked about it. But most of us grew up the same way — you know lower middle class, middle class, listening to a lot of the same music, struggling, especially studio guys I knew from everywhere. I always likened it to this mob of people trying to get through a keyhole to be a studio musician, and just a few at a time can slip through. Everybody wanted to do it. I always said, I was just talking about this yesterday, that most of the time when you go out and see somebody on the road playing concerts, that’s not the people that played on the record. It’s a road band. Everybody out on the road wants to be a studio musician, or at least used to be. They all wanted to be in the studio. They did this hoping that it was going to lead to that. And I always likened it to a mob trying to get through a keyhole. And we all grew up, and we came from everywhere, just like actors and actresses that flocked to Hollywood. We went to music centers, whether it was Nashville, Memphis, Muscle Shoals, New York, L.A. Detroit, Philadelphia. We came from everywhere and found each other. And we were let in through the keyhole. And we all had similar backgrounds. Some of the guys I know, like Hungate, we spoke about David Hungate earlier, North Texas State, that great One O’clock Jump Jazz Band, he could read everything, but his father was a judge up in Indiana. But David, believe me, once he got out of North Texas State and went to L.A., he had to work his way up the ranks. I mean Toto was one thing, but they were all studio, young studio guys, Porcaro and Hungate and all those guys. They all had to compete and prove themselves, like all of us did.
